coverageNote: An intentionally incomplete first diligence cohort chosen to test direct service, advocacy, LGBTQ+ community support, food security, housing, and multi-service models. Inclusion is not a recommendation.

rules.discovery: Candidate discovery is not a recommendation. A headquarters address, public contract, Charity Navigator profile, or self-reported impact claim does not establish marginal impact.
rules.publicFunding: Contract figures are life-to-date accounting fields from the MFI-019 snapshot. They can reveal public-funding overlap but not effectiveness, displacement, or philanthropic room for more funding.
rules.ratings: Charity Navigator ratings are preserved with completed-beacon coverage when published. They are governance, finance, and sometimes measurement signals—not Market for Impact effectiveness scores.
rules.causality: Organization-reported outputs and policy or election wins remain contribution evidence unless an independent counterfactual design supports an outcome claim.
rules.conversion: QALY and WELLBY estimates are blocked for every candidate until a versioned local model, defensible counterfactual, and uncertainty analysis exist.

candidates.name: Hamilton Families
candidates.donationDeductibility: Organization states donations are tax-deductible to the extent allowed by law.
candidates.serviceGeography: San Francisco Bay Area; current city contracts confirm San Francisco programs.
candidates.interventionType: family homelessness prevention, shelter, rapid rehousing, and housing subsidies
candidates.theoryOfChange: Temporary assistance, landlord partnerships, shelter, and case management can prevent displacement or help families move into stable housing; child supports may reduce education disruption.
candidates.evidenceSummary: The April–June 2026 report states 338 families served, 34 program exits to stable housing, 19 families receiving eviction-prevention assistance, and $660,709 in housing subsidies.
candidates.causalBoundary: The report supplies service and exit counts, but no comparison group, durability follow-up, cost per sustained housing outcome, or donor-attribution estimate.
candidates.marginalFunding: No reviewed, time-bounded marginal funding gap or next-dollar plan is published in the accepted sources.
candidates.downsideCase: Subsidies may replace public dollars or move families between programs without increasing durable housing supply; housing exits may not persist.

charityNavigator.note: The displayed overall score is based on Accountability & Finance only; it is not an impact estimate.

evidenceDossier.scope: Hamilton Families' homelessness-prevention and rapid-rehousing work; not every program or every geography the organization serves.
evidenceDossier.decisionSummary: Hamilton reports substantial family-housing activity and has unusually relevant external research, but no accepted source yet identifies the durable, additional outcomes a new gift would buy. The evidence supports a serious diligence conversation, not a ranked recommendation.

outcomes.label: Families reported to have avoided homelessness
outcomes.limitation: No comparison group or counterfactual identifies how many families would otherwise have entered homelessness.

outcomes.label: Families reported to have maintained housing
outcomes.limitation: The reviewed report does not provide a common follow-up window or comparison-group rate.

outcomes.label: Newly housed within the maintained-housing count
outcomes.limitation: This is a subset of 344, not an additional outcome count.

outcomes.label: Average intake-to-placement time
outcomes.limitation: The report does not isolate the drivers of the change or connect it to durable housing stability.

financials.boundary: Organization-wide audited-period totals are scale and funding-mix context. They do not identify program-level marginal cost, room for more funding, or San Francisco-only spending.

evidenceLayers.title: Toward a Geographic Strategy for Rapid Re-housing
evidenceLayers.finding: The analysis examined where Hamilton's Heading Home Initiative might place families in a high-cost, low-vacancy region and documented the initiative's planned scale.
evidenceLayers.decisionUse: Useful for testing placement strategy and whether evidence from easier housing markets transfers to the Bay Area.
evidenceLayers.transferLimit: Hamilton funded the work with Salesforce.org support. It is not an outcome impact evaluation and provides no Hamilton-specific causal effect.

evidenceLayers.title: Bay Area Thriving Families
evidenceLayers.design: randomized controlled trial; 450-family target, $1,000 versus $50 monthly for 12 months, two-year follow-up
evidenceLayers.finding: No outcome results were published on the accepted source as of the review date.
evidenceLayers.decisionUse: The eventual results may clarify whether post-program unrestricted cash improves stability after rapid rehousing.
evidenceLayers.transferLimit: The intervention is cash after rapid rehousing, not an evaluation of Hamilton's full service model.

evidenceLayers.publisher: U.S. Department of Housing and Urban Development
evidenceLayers.title: Family Options Study
evidenceLayers.design: multisite randomized controlled trial; 2,282 families across 12 communities
evidenceLayers.finding: Long-term housing subsidies produced the broadest benefits. Community-based rapid rehousing showed little broad improvement over usual care in housing stability and family wellbeing at the study's follow-ups.
evidenceLayers.decisionUse: Raises the evidence bar for assuming that a time-limited rapid-rehousing offer creates durable gains beyond services otherwise available.
evidenceLayers.transferLimit: This older, multisite study is not Hamilton-specific; implementation varied and the sites do not reproduce today's Bay Area housing market.

evidenceLayers.publisher: U.S. Department of Housing and Urban Development
evidenceLayers.title: Rapid Re-housing for Homeless Families Demonstration Programs Evaluation
evidenceLayers.finding: HUD reports that 10% returned to homelessness and 76% moved at least once within 12 months; programs varied substantially in assistance and services.
evidenceLayers.decisionUse: Useful for choosing durability and residential-mobility measures for Hamilton-specific follow-up.
evidenceLayers.transferLimit: Without a counterfactual, the reported rates do not establish program impact or predict Hamilton's results.

missingForRecommendation: A common 12- and 24-month housing-stability denominator, including returns to homelessness and moves.
Program-level cost per sustained housing outcome, with public and private funding reconciled.
A time-bounded marginal plan at $100,000, $1 million, and $10 million, including capacity constraints and displacement risk.
Evidence about which families are additional to public or usual-care pathways and what the next donor dollar changes.
Results from the Bay Area Thriving Families trial, interpreted only for its post-rapid-rehousing cash intervention.

candidates.name: San Francisco–Marin Food Bank
candidates.donationDeductibility: Tax-deductible charitable vehicle; confirm individual circumstances with the organization or an adviser.
candidates.serviceGeography: San Francisco and Marin counties; this scorecard isolates the organization but not all reported activity to San Francisco.
candidates.interventionType: food distribution, community markets, benefits access, and food-policy advocacy
candidates.theoryOfChange: Reliable access to nutritious food can reduce food insecurity and free household resources for housing and other essentials; benefits enrollment and policy advocacy may address upstream causes.
candidates.evidenceSummary: The FY2025 report identifies 265 community partners and reports $159.4M in program-service expense, including substantial donated-food value. It describes a transition from pop-up pantries to community markets.
candidates.causalBoundary: Distributed-food value, meals, partners, and program expense are not equivalent to households becoming food secure. The reviewed report does not publish a counterfactual or SF-only cost per durable outcome.
candidates.marginalFunding: The report describes growing demand and flexible private support but does not publish a bounded marginal gap, capacity ceiling, or incremental outcome schedule.
candidates.downsideCase: Food distribution may manage acute need without changing root causes; donated-food accounting can dominate dollar totals and obscure cash marginal cost.

charityNavigator.note: Three completed beacons improve signal coverage, but the rating still is not a causal or marginal impact estimate.

evidenceDossier.scope: San Francisco–Marin Food Bank's grocery access, home-delivery, community-market, and benefits-enrollment work; not every partner program or policy activity.
evidenceDossier.decisionSummary: The Food Bank has exceptional local reach and credible evidence that more intensive pantry models can improve short-term food security. Its own published evidence, however, remains dominated by delivery counts, participant surveys, and organization-wide accounting. No accepted source yet shows the durable, additional food-security outcome purchased by a new private gift.

outcomes.label: Households served weekly across two counties
outcomes.limitation: A weekly service count is not a unique annual household denominator or a measure of becoming food secure; San Francisco and Marin are combined.

outcomes.label: Meals-equivalent food shared
outcomes.limitation: A standardized meals-equivalent converts food volume, not meals eaten, nutrition gained, or food insecurity reduced.

outcomes.label: Community Market participants
outcomes.limitation: The two new markets reported reach but no comparison group, sustained food-security measure, or incremental cost.

outcomes.label: CalFresh benefits secured through application help
outcomes.limitation: The report does not publish approval persistence, a comparison with unassisted applicants, or the share attributable to Food Bank assistance.

financials.boundary: Organization-wide totals include $83.9 million of donated food and in-kind value. They do not reveal cash cost per household, program-specific marginal cost, San Francisco-only spending, or room for more funding.

evidenceLayers.publisher: City and County of San Francisco
evidenceLayers.title: FY2022–2023 service and outcome performance
evidenceLayers.design: contract monitoring plus voluntary participant survey
evidenceLayers.finding: City staff reported 50,214 grocery units and 18,884 unduplicated households per month against lower contract targets. In a survey completed by 21% of participants, 96% reported decreased food insecurity.
evidenceLayers.decisionUse: Confirms that the contracted grocery program delivered substantial volume and identifies a food-security measure worth following prospectively.
evidenceLayers.transferLimit: The survey was voluntary, had no comparison group, and covered an earlier pandemic-era program configuration. Self-reported improvement cannot be assigned to a new donor dollar.

evidenceLayers.title: Home-Delivered Grocery Programs: Impact and Opportunities
evidenceLayers.design: program landscape analysis with preliminary survey of more than 800 participants
evidenceLayers.finding: The report states that 93% of surveyed home-delivery participants worried less about getting enough food and describes access barriers for seniors, people with disabilities, and families with young children.
evidenceLayers.decisionUse: Supports home delivery as a distinct access intervention and identifies target populations and delivery constraints for deeper diligence.
evidenceLayers.transferLimit: The Food Bank published the analysis; the preliminary survey had no counterfactual and does not establish durable health or food-security effects.

evidenceLayers.title: A systematic review of food pantry-based interventions in the USA
evidenceLayers.design: systematic review; 14 articles covering 12 interventions, including five randomized trials
evidenceLayers.finding: The review found improvements across several diet-related outcomes, especially for client-choice, nutrition, display, and diabetes-management interventions.
evidenceLayers.decisionUse: Supports testing specific enhanced pantry components rather than treating food distribution volume as an outcome.
evidenceLayers.transferLimit: Interventions and outcomes were too heterogeneous for meta-analysis; studies were generally modest, short, and vulnerable to subjective measures and publication bias.

evidenceLayers.title: A novel food pantry program: food security, self-sufficiency, and diet-quality outcomes
evidenceLayers.design: randomized trial; 228 adults followed for 12 months
evidenceLayers.finding: Participants offered Freshplace—a client-choice pantry plus monthly case management and targeted referrals—were less than half as likely to experience very low food security and reported higher self-sufficiency and produce intake than traditional-pantry controls.
evidenceLayers.decisionUse: Provides a credible causal benchmark for a bundled, higher-touch pantry model resembling some Community Market ambitions.
evidenceLayers.transferLimit: Freshplace was a Connecticut program with case management and referrals; it is not an evaluation of SF–Marin's current markets, network, or marginal funding opportunity.

missingForRecommendation: A unique-participant denominator with a common 6- and 12-month USDA food-security measure, separated by program and county.
Cash and in-kind cost per sustained food-security outcome, rather than cost per pound or meals-equivalent distributed.
A time-bounded marginal plan at $100,000, $1 million, and $10 million, including food supply, partner, warehouse, volunteer, and delivery capacity.
A reconciliation of private gifts with city contracts, government commodities, donated-food inventory, and likely displacement of other funders.
Prospective evaluation of Community Markets or home delivery against the current pantry or usual-service alternative.

candidates.name: SF LGBT Center
candidates.donationDeductibility: The organization identifies itself as a 501(c)(3); employer matching may be available.
candidates.serviceGeography: San Francisco and Bay Area LGBTQ+ communities; city contracts include employment, youth, and community services.
candidates.interventionType: LGBTQ+ youth services, employment and financial coaching, referrals, community space, and advocacy
candidates.theoryOfChange: Integrated affirming services and a trusted community hub may improve economic security, connection, housing stability, and access to mental-health support for LGBTQ+ residents.
candidates.evidenceSummary: The audited program description identifies economic-development, youth, community, and building-service programs. Current city contracts confirm employment, financial-coaching, youth, and social-service activity.
candidates.causalBoundary: The accepted sources do not yet provide a reconciled outcome denominator, counterfactual, sustained follow-up, or cost per economic, housing, or health outcome.
candidates.marginalFunding: No reviewed program-specific marginal gap or capacity schedule is published; donation and matching routes are available.
candidates.downsideCase: A broad service portfolio makes organization-level attribution difficult; public contracts may already fund some activities donors assume are marginal.
contractAliases: THE SAN FRANCISCO LGBT COMMUNITY CENTER
grantLedgerAliases: San Francisco Lesbian Gay Bisexual Transgender Community Center

charityNavigator.note: The profile reports a four-star rating; completed-beacon count was not captured, so this is not treated as comprehensive effectiveness evidence.

sources.title: The Center: impact and financial transparency
sources.period: Current page; 2025 review and FY2024 audit linked

evidenceDossier.scope: The SF LGBT Center's employment, financial, housing-navigation, and youth mental-health services; not every cultural, community, facility, or advocacy activity.
evidenceDossier.decisionSummary: The Center publishes unusually legible service counts and has invested in a center-wide measurement framework. Its strongest reported economic outcomes—living-wage job placements and first-time home purchases—still lack common follow-up, comparison rates, program-level cost, and a marginal funding plan. External research supports testing specific employment and youth-housing components, not assigning impact to the Center's broad portfolio.

outcomes.label: LGBTQ+ job seekers receiving employment support
outcomes.limitation: The report combines drop-in support, workshops, mentorship, and one-to-one assistance without a unique-service intensity or comparison-group denominator.

outcomes.label: Community members securing living-wage employment
outcomes.limitation: The report does not define the wage threshold, follow-up window, job retention, baseline placement rate, or which services preceded each placement.

outcomes.label: First-time homebuyers
outcomes.limitation: The report does not identify the counterfactual purchase rate, time to close, Center-attributable contribution, or cost per additional homebuyer.

outcomes.label: Gender-affirming youth mental-health support
outcomes.limitation: Hours delivered are not a mental-health outcome; the report does not publish a validated symptom or well-being measure with follow-up.

financials.revenueNote: $3.62M government grants · $2.06M donations/foundations/events · $0.86M facility and program revenue
financials.boundary: FY2024 organization-wide audited totals allocate expenses across four broad program families. They do not reveal cost per retained job, additional homebuyer, sustained housing outcome, or improved youth mental health; government grants supplied 55% of reported revenue and require program-level displacement analysis.

evidenceLayers.publisher: SF LGBT Center and Intention 2 Impact
evidenceLayers.title: 2024–2025 Monitoring, Evaluation, and Learning framework
evidenceLayers.design: center-wide theory-of-change process with surveys, focus groups, and interviews involving 248 community members
evidenceLayers.finding: Participants described the Center as safe, affirming, culturally competent, and important for connection; the process produced a theory of change and a commitment to collect and share outcomes regularly.
evidenceLayers.decisionUse: Establishes participant-valued mechanisms and a concrete measurement roadmap that future grants can attach to.
evidenceLayers.transferLimit: The Center commissioned and published the work; it is a formative, self-selected mixed-methods evaluation without a comparison group, quantified durable outcomes, program costs, or donor counterfactual.

evidenceLayers.title: Interventions to improve the labour market outcomes of youth
evidenceLayers.design: systematic review of 107 experimental or quasi-experimental interventions in 31 countries
evidenceLayers.finding: Youth employment programs produced small average gains with substantial variation; entrepreneurship promotion and skills training showed positive effects, while employment-service effects were negligible or statistically insignificant on average.
evidenceLayers.decisionUse: Supports separating the Center's training, entrepreneurship, coaching, career-fair, and placement components and measuring retained employment and earnings by component.
evidenceLayers.transferLimit: The review was not LGBTQ+-specific, mixed high- and lower-income settings, and does not identify the effect of the Center's employment services or San Francisco labor-market context.

evidenceLayers.title: Housing and Support Interventions for Homeless Youth in High-Income Countries
evidenceLayers.design: systematic review of five North American counterfactual studies reported across 19 papers
evidenceLayers.finding: Some interventions improved housing stability in the short term, but effects often diminished; health, social, education, and employment estimates were mixed or imprecise.
evidenceLayers.decisionUse: Identifies durable housing stability, service intensity, fidelity, and 6- to 24-month follow-up as requirements for evaluating youth housing-navigation support.
evidenceLayers.transferLimit: The studies had non-ignorable risk of bias, heterogeneous measures prevented synthesis, and subgroup evidence for gender and sexual minority youth remained insufficient; none evaluated the Center.

evidenceLayers.title: A systematic review of experimental evidence on interventions against bias and discrimination in organizations
evidenceLayers.design: systematic review of 116 experimental papers covering 159 interventions from 2000–2022
evidenceLayers.finding: Structural interventions and structured procedures or interactions showed promise for reducing bias affecting sexual minorities; exposure interventions also produced positive effects in some settings.
evidenceLayers.decisionUse: Suggests that employer-facing process changes may be a distinct intervention worth measuring alongside job-seeker coaching and placement.
evidenceLayers.transferLimit: The review spans several protected characteristics, interventions, settings, and intermediate bias measures; it does not establish employment or earnings effects for the Center's clients.

missingForRecommendation: Program-level unique-participant cohorts with baseline characteristics and common 6- and 12-month employment, earnings, housing, and mental-health outcomes.
Cost per retained living-wage job, additional homebuyer, sustained housing outcome, or validated youth mental-health improvement—not cost per contact or service hour.
A time-bounded marginal plan at $100,000, $1 million, and $10 million, including staff, employer, housing, facility, and referral capacity.
A reconciliation of private gifts with the five active city contracts, government grants, restricted funding, and likely displacement of other funders.
A credible counterfactual or phased evaluation for the specific employment, financial, housing, or youth intervention a donor would expand.

candidates.name: GLIDE
candidates.donationDeductibility: The accepted profile identifies GLIDE Foundation as a 501(c)(3); donors should select the intended GLIDE entity.
candidates.serviceGeography: Tenderloin, San Francisco, and the broader Bay Area; city contracts confirm multiple local programs.
candidates.interventionType: meals, housing navigation, behavioral health, family programs, outreach, and advocacy
candidates.theoryOfChange: Low-barrier, integrated services can meet immediate needs and create pathways into housing, health, and family stability while advocacy addresses structural barriers.
candidates.evidenceSummary: The FY2025 report describes a roughly $30.8M expense base and multiple frontline programs. Current city contracts link GLIDE to meals, housing navigation, youth, health, and ambassador services.
candidates.causalBoundary: Organization-wide service and financial totals cannot be assigned to one outcome. The accepted sources do not establish a donor counterfactual or cost per sustained local outcome.
candidates.marginalFunding: The report argues private unrestricted support enables responsiveness, but publishes no bounded gap, program capacity curve, or incremental outcome estimate.
candidates.downsideCase: Breadth can dilute measurement and create double-counting across connected services; some reported FY2025 financials were marked pending final audit in the impact report.

charityNavigator.note: Charity Navigator currently displays GLIDE Foundation as not rated; absence of a rating is not a negative impact finding.

nativeSignals.signalType: financial; report marked pending final audit

nativeSignals.signalType: financial; report marked pending final audit

candidates.name: GrowSF
candidates.donationDeductibility: GrowSF states donations are not deductible as charitable contributions for federal income-tax purposes.
candidates.interventionType: voter information, candidate support, policy research, and electoral advocacy
candidates.theoryOfChange: Research, voter guides, and campaigns may change officeholders and ballot outcomes, which may in turn change policy implementation and long-run city outcomes.
candidates.evidenceSummary: GrowSF reports 117,000 unique voter-guide visitors and victories for every supported June 2026 candidate, along with campaign-channel spending and reach.
candidates.causalBoundary: Reach and aligned election results do not identify how many votes GrowSF changed, the counterfactual result, implementation quality, or downstream housing, safety, education, or economic outcomes.
candidates.marginalFunding: Donation asks and campaign uses are visible, but no reviewed marginal dollars-to-votes or policy-outcome curve is published.
candidates.downsideCase: Electoral activity is value-laden and may create policy harms as well as benefits; donor preferences, campaign-finance rules, and non-deductibility differ from charitable giving.

candidates.name: Housing Action Coalition
candidates.donationDeductibility: HAC states only contributions to its 501(c)(3) education and research vehicle are tax-deductible to the extent allowed by law; advocacy gifts use its 501(c)(4).
candidates.serviceGeography: California with Bay Area and San Francisco advocacy; reported impacts are not SF-only.
candidates.interventionType: housing policy research, project endorsements, coalition building, litigation strategy, and legislative advocacy
candidates.theoryOfChange: Policy and legal advocacy can make more housing legally feasible and reduce approval barriers, potentially increasing completions and moderating long-run housing costs.
candidates.evidenceSummary: The 2024 report attributes more than 100 acres of rezoning and legal capacity for more than 4,500 multifamily units to its Housing Element accountability work with counsel.
candidates.causalBoundary: Legally feasible units are not permits, starts, completions, occupied homes, affordability changes, or SF-only outcomes. Contribution among coalition partners is not independently apportioned.
candidates.marginalFunding: The donation page describes policy, coalition, and advocacy uses but gives no time-bounded gap or marginal policy-win forecast.
candidates.downsideCase: Upzoning may not produce construction in weak markets and can create distributional tradeoffs; policy attribution is especially vulnerable to coalition double-counting.
